Nomura: The Midterm Elections Won't Help, Only the Fed CanmarsbitPublished on 2026-11-01Last updated on 2026-11-01AbstractNomura strategist Naka Matsuzawa argues that the U.S. midterm elections will not be the catalyst that ends the global tech selloff, contrary to widespread market hopes. In his October 30 macro strategy note, he contends that election results matter far less to equities than expected, and that the only real catalyst capable of halting the tech decline is the Federal Reserve ending its rate-hiking cycle.

Matsuzawa attributes tech weakness not to election uncertainty but to two deeper drivers: mounting concerns over the sustainability of AI investment and persistent credit worries. He notes that event premiums around the midterms in futures markets have already fallen noticeably, and that companies expected to face tighter regulation have not visibly underperformed—evidence that the selloff is not directly tied to regulatory fears. Investors, he observes, are punishing earnings misses harshly while giving little credit to beats, and they favor restrained capex, improved cash flow and shareholder returns over aggressive spending, reflecting deep anxiety about an AI investment slowdown.

Recent sector moves—a rebound in semiconductors (SOX up 6.9% for the week) alongside weakness in hyperscalers and software—do not, in his view, constitute meaningful rotation, since capital goods and machinery stocks, typically leading indicators of AI investment recovery, remain subdued. bonuses.requirements: 0 Layoffs, Expert Salaries Cut 30% First, DeepMind Co-Founder Predicts AI’s First Strike | HTX InsightsHomeCrypto News0 Layoffs, Expert Salaries Cut...0 Layoffs, Expert Salaries Cut 30% First, DeepMind Co-Founder Predicts AI’s First StrikemarsbitPublished on 2026-11-02Last updated on 2026-11-02AbstractDeepMind co-founder Shane Legg, along with AGI economics director Alex Imas and researcher Andrew Koh, published "The Economics of Intelligence" and the working paper "Organizing Intelligence," arguing that AI's economic impact will hit wages before employment. The paper divides AI evolution into four stages: Minimal AGI, Supercompetent AI, Supercooperative AI, and ASI. Using a 14-person model economy (6 programmers, 6 writers, 2 coordinators), they show that even when no one is laid off, once AI matches average human ability, specialist wages fall about 30% and coordinator wages 46%, because scarcity disappears—AI can be replicated infinitely at compute cost, anchoring wages to compute prices. When AI surpasses all human experts ("Supercompetent"), specialist wages collapse over 90%, while low-scoring coordinators become the highest paid. The authors introduce "mosaic intelligence": humans are jagged specialists whose complementary teamwork beats individual ability, and a single model copied many times cannot fill skill gaps. Multi-agent AI systems currently fail badly at collaboration (41–87% task failure rates), creating a "Coasean ceiling" that protects human firms. But once AI collaboration capability crosses 1 ("Supercooperative"), returns to scale turn increasing, and production concentrates into a giant pure-AI firm—a "corporate singularity." At that point even coordinators lose out, with about half unemployed at supercooperation and all gone at ASI. Non-qualified investors can buy up to 300,000 rubles (about $3,700) in crypto annually through each intermediary, including brokers, asset managers and crypto exchange providers. Qualified investors face no purchase limits, but all investors must pass a mandatory test before trading. The directive builds on legislation signed by President Vladimir Putin on Aug. 4 establishing a regulated crypto market under central bank oversight. On Aug. 11, the Bank of Russia published draft regulations identifying BTC, ETH and USDT as eligible for public trading based on market capitalization, average daily trading volume and at least five years of price history on foreign exchanges. The law took effect Sept. 1, and the Bank of Russia later authorized Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to offer crypto exchange services in October. Moscow Exchange, Russia’s largest securities exchange and a publicly traded company, is preparing to launch crypto trading on Dec. 1, initially offering the three cryptocurrencies through pilot transactions. Previously, chat and coding had separate allowances; now both draw from a single shared pool, and usage will be measured in tokens rather than message counts. Only Instant chat remains unlimited. Users can check remaining quota and reset times under Settings → Usage, and when exhausted they can wait for a reset, upgrade, or buy credits. OpenAI has not specified an exact launch date or token amounts per tier.

The change follows a month of frequent quota resets and Codex updates led by Tibo (Thibault Sottiaux), who ran a 28-day challenge of daily improvements or full resets. During that period OpenAI doubled quotas for Pro 100/200/500 and Business Premium, but not Plus, drawing complaints. Tibo's remark about graduating from "The Reset Company" to "The Token Company" now looks like a preview of the pooled, token-based model.

Separately, OpenAI tightened device limits: a single device can use only a limited number of paid accounts across Go, Plus, and Pro tiers, with excess logins showing "Device limit reached" or being logged out. This undercuts users who rotated multiple subscriptions, just as multi-account switching arrived on mobile. Community reaction has been negative, with some Plus users saying they may buy more Claude instead, since independent chat quota was a key attraction.
